t: Some reactions would take a thousand years on their own. A cell does them a thousand times a second.
Left alone in water, some of the reactions your cells depend on would take millions of years. The same reaction inside you happens thousands of times a second, at body temperature.
sub: Nothing is being heated up. So what changed?
No extra energy is supplied and the products are identical. Something else has been altered.

question: How can a cell speed a reaction up without heating anything?
What can accelerate a reaction by a factor of a million without supplying energy?
options: Hold the pieces in exactly the right position
stages.outcome: Hold the pieces in exactly the right position
note: Commit. Note that heating would speed it up too — and would also cook the cell, which is the constraint that rules it out.

stages.label: Try each shape in the notch
captions: Too big. It will not go in.
Too small. It rattles around and nothing happens.
Right size, wrong shape. Still no.
It fits. The reaction happens instantly.
t: The enzyme has a notch in it. Try each shape and see which one fits.
The pocket accepts one shape and refuses the rest. Work through them.
after: Only one shape fits, and that is why the enzyme only does one job.
One substrate, one pocket. Specificity and catalysis come from the same feature.

stages.label: Temperature
captions: 0 °C: molecules barely meet. Almost no activity.
37 °C: maximum. Every enzyme in you is tuned to about here.
50 °C: activity falling — and the enzyme is starting to unfold.
60 °C: unfolded and aggregated. Activity is zero and does not come back.
t: Enzymes speed up with heat like any reaction — up to a point. Find the point and work out what is happening on each side of it.
Two competing effects sit either side of the optimum. Identify both, and note that only one of them is reversible.
after: Rising because collisions get faster; falling because the shape comes apart.

Collision frequency rises smoothly with temperature; denaturation is a cooperative transition that sets in sharply. The optimum is where the second overtakes the first — and unlike the first, it does not reverse on cooling.

t: A protein that speeds up a reaction is called an enzyme. The notch is its active site.
A protein that catalyses a reaction is an enzyme, and the pocket it does it in is the active site.
Enzymes are catalysts: they lower the activation energy of a reaction without being consumed and without altering its equilibrium.

The mechanism is not simply holding the substrate — it is binding the transition state more tightly than the substrate itself. Pauling's insight in 1948, and the reason transition-state analogues make such effective drugs.
sub: It only fits one thing, so it only does one job.
Specificity comes free with the mechanism: the pocket that positions one molecule correctly cannot accommodate another.
An enzyme changes the rate, never the direction. It cannot make an unfavourable reaction happen — only a slow favourable one fast.

That constraint is absolute and worth holding onto: catalysis is kinetic. An enzyme accelerates approach to equilibrium in both directions equally, which is why the same enzyme often runs a pathway forwards and backwards depending only on concentrations.

q: Why does an enzyme only do one job?
What is the basis of enzyme specificity?
Why are specificity and catalysis inseparable?
options: Because only one shape fits its notch
Because it only meets one kind of molecule
why: The notch is a particular shape. Only a molecule that matches it can get in, so that is the only reaction it can help with.

The active site's geometry is what positions a substrate correctly, and a pocket shaped to fit one molecule precisely cannot fit another. Specificity is not a separate feature — it is the same feature.

Catalytic power comes from complementarity to the transition state, and complementarity is by definition exclusive. An enzyme that accepted many substrates would position none of them well enough to accelerate anything, so promiscuity and efficiency trade off directly.

t: Lots of medicines work by sitting in an enzyme's notch so nothing else can.

Competitive inhibition is one of the most productive strategies in pharmacology: statins occupy the active site of the enzyme that makes cholesterol, and many antivirals block the protease a virus needs to cut its own proteins apart. In both cases the drug is a shape designed to fit a pocket and do nothing once it is there.

q: Why does activity fall above the optimum temperature?
Why is the fall in activity above the optimum not simply the reverse of the rise?
options: The enzyme is unfolding, and that does not reverse on cooling
The reaction runs out of substrate
The molecules move too fast to collide
why: Below the peak, more heat means more collisions and more reaction. Above it, the heat is shaking the protein apart — and once it has unfolded and stuck to its neighbours, cooling it down does not bring it back.

The two effects are asymmetric in kind. Collision frequency is a smooth reversible function of temperature; denaturation is a cooperative transition that destroys the active site and is usually followed by irreversible aggregation. That asymmetry is why the curve is not a symmetric peak, and why a fever above about 42 °C is dangerous rather than merely uncomfortable.
